This bar stands for the independent states of sub-Saharan Africa from 1957, when Ghana became the first colony south of the Sahara to win independence, to the present. (Ethiopia and Liberia had never been colonies in the usual sense, and Sudan became independent in 1956.)

Independence came in waves:

  • 1957: Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah.
  • 1958: Guinea voted against staying in a French community and became independent at once.
  • 1960: the Year of Africa, with seventeen new states, most of them former French colonies, plus Nigeria, the Belgian Congo and Somalia.
  • 1961 to 1968: most British colonies in East and Central Africa, including Kenya in 1963 after the Mau Mau war.
  • 1975: Mozambique and Angola, after long wars against Portugal.
  • 1980 Zimbabwe, 1990 Namibia, and in 1994 majority rule in South Africa under Nelson Mandela.

The new states mostly kept the borders drawn in the colonial era, and the Organisation of African Unity agreed in 1964 to respect them. Former French colonies kept close ties to France, including the CFA franc.

The first decades were hard. Many states became one-party regimes or fell to military coups, and the Cold War powers backed rival sides in civil wars, from the Congo Crisis of 1960 to Angola. Famine and the AIDS epidemic hit hard in places. Since the 1990s multiparty elections have spread, and the population has grown faster than anywhere else in the world. The bar continues the story of decolonisation into the present.
